newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Woo's bid for HK leadership draws mixed response.
newsitem.headline: Woo's bid for HK leadership draws mixed response.

text.p: The latest candidate to enter the race to become Hong Kong's leader when the British leave next year attracted a mixed response from Hong Kong commentators on Tuesday.

Peter Woo, son-in-law of the late Hong Kong shipping magnate Sir Yue-kong Pao, announced his candidacy on Monday for the future top job in Hong Kong once it reverts to Chinese rule on July 1, 1997, after more than 150 years as a British colony.
In recent years, Woo has turned his back on business to concentrate on public service.

Woo, 50, remains honorary chairman of Wharf (Holdings) Ltd and Wheelock and Co Ltd, but has stepped back from day-to-day running of his companies to become chairman of Hong Kong's Hospital Authority, responsible for public infirmaries.

"I think Peter Woo has his own merits in the sense that he has something which might not necessarily be possessed by other candidates," said Lau Siu-kai, an academic and a member of China's Preparatory Committee overseeing the handover.

"For example, he's pretty young...and he has been pretty enterprising in his business and he has been actively involved in the public service and he gives people the impression that he is a reformer rather than a conservative," Lau added.

Some newspapers reported David Chu, another member of China's hand-picked Preparatory Committee, had also complimented Woo's performance at the Hospital Authority, saying his public services showed his sincerity to society.

The Preparatory Committee, made up of local and Chinese appointees, is responsible for devising a process to select the post-1997 legislature and chief executive, replacing colonial governor Chris Patten.
But Woo also had his shortcomings, commentators said.
"He might be seen as too young for a Chinese politician and ...he might not be fully trusted by China yet at the present moment," Lau said.

"And I think being a businessman he might also be seen as too much entangled in British interests and might be opposed by other businessmen for being a threat to their own interests once he becomes the chief executive," he said.
The Hong Kong Economic Times newspaper questioned how Woo would account for his pledge to support Patten's political reforms, which are fiercely opposed by Beijing.
Woo is the fifth person to weigh into the race for Hong Kong's post-colonial leadership.
Shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa, widely tipped as Beijing's favourite, has also said he was considering running for the post.
Local newspapers compared Woo and Tung, noting their similar backgrounds.
Woo and Tung were both born in Shanghai, educated in the West, are successors to shipping tycoons, ran large businesses and had extensive international connections, the Economic Journal reported.
But Woo had a more straightforward style resembling western politicians while Tung was more traditional, the paper said.
The Sing Tao Daily newspaper said some Preparatory Committee members felt Woo was joining the race to divert support from Tung.
Popularity polls put Patten's deputy Anson Chan far ahead of the five contenders, although she has not declared her candidacy.
Former Chief Justice Sir Ti Liang Yang ranks second in the popularity stakes ahead of lawyer Lo Tak-shing.
However, popularity is not an issue in the choice for first post-handover leader, who will be picked by a 400-strong body to be named by the Preparatory Committee.
Lau expected more candidates to come forward for the post.
